blocks.md: **The US income Gini traces a U: high in the 1920s, a sharp compression into the 1940s, three flat decades, then a steady rise from about 1980 to well above the 1920s peak.**
Values are read off the lecture's charts and are approximate.

| Period | US Gini (tax units) | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1917 | ≈ 0.51 | |
| 1928–29 | ≈ 0.57 | Pre-Depression peak |
| Early 1940s | ≈ 0.40 | Trough — the "Great Compression" |
| 1950s–1970s | ≈ 0.43–0.47 | Slow drift up, no big moves |
| 1980 | ≈ 0.48 | Start of the modern rise |
| Late 1980s | ≈ 0.58 | Steepest climb |
| 2000 | ≈ 0.60 | |
| 2012–2015 | ≈ 0.64 | Above the 1929 peak |
California and New York follow the same U but sit higher:

- **California**: trough ≈ 0.36 around 1940; ≈ 0.68 by the 2010s
- **New York**: ≈ 0.65 in 1929; trough ≈ 0.42; ≈ 0.71 by the 2010s — the most unequal of the three

This is a Gini of **tax-unit income** over **tax filers** ([IRS Individual Tax Data](note:irs-individual-tax-data)). It is not comparable with survey-based family-income Ginis — see [Cross-Country Gini Comparison](note:cross-country-gini-comparison), where the US scores 45.0. Same country, different variable and population ([Defining Inequality](note:defining-inequality)).
